Explore how GitHub Actions, Vale, and Lychee automate prose linting, broken link detection, and preview deployments.

import { Aside, Tabs, TabItem, Steps, Code } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

In a traditional documentation workflow, quality control is manual, error-prone, and relies entirely on human review. Typos slip into production, external hyperlinks rot over time, and formatting inconsistencies degrade the professional quality of the knowledge base.

This architecture replaces manual auditing with **automated quality gates**. Using GitHub Actions, every single pull request is automatically tested for prose style, link integrity, and build validity before a human ever clicks "Merge."

---

## The Automated Pipeline Architecture

Whenever a contributor pushes code or submits changes via Sveltia CMS, GitHub Actions fires off three parallel verification jobs:

<Steps>
  1. **Prose Linting (Vale)**
     Scans all Markdown and MDX files against the Google Developer Style Guide to catch passive voice, jargon, and spelling inconsistencies.
  2. **Link Integrity Check (Lychee)**
     Crawls every internal and external hyperlink across the site to ensure zero 404 errors or broken URLs exist.
  3. **Preview Deployment (Astro Build)**
     Performs a full static build of the site to verify that MDX components, frontmatter schemas, and content collections compile cleanly.
</Steps>

---

## Behind the Configuration

Explore the implementation files that drive these quality checks behind the scenes.

<Tabs>
  <TabItem label="1. Vale (Prose Linter)" icon="seti:config">
    *Enforcing editorial standards using `.vale.ini`.*

    Vale analyzes natural language text just like a compiler analyzes source code. Our configuration points to the Google Style Guide to ensure concise, active, and accessible technical writing.

    ```ini title=".vale.ini"
    StylesPath = .vale/styles
    MinAlertLevel = warning

    [*.mdx]
    BasedOnStyles = Google
    
    # Custom overrides
    Google.We = suggestion
    ```
  </TabItem>

  <TabItem label="2. Lychee (Link Checker)" icon="seti:config">
    *Preventing link rot using `lychee.toml`.*

    Lychee is a fast, async link checker written in Rust. It scans all generated HTML output during CI to verify that referenced resources are online and responsive.

    ```toml title="lychee.toml"
    verbose = true
    accept = [200, 429]
    timeout = 10
    exclude_all_private = true
    ```
  </TabItem>

  <TabItem label="3. GitHub Actions CI" icon="github">
    *Orchestrating the pipeline via `.github/workflows/ci.yml`.*

    ```yaml title=".github/workflows/ci.yml"
    name: Docs CI & Quality Gates

    on:
      pull_request:
        branches: [ main ]
      push:
        branches: [ main ]

    jobs:
      validate:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - name: Checkout Repository
            uses: actions/checkout@v4

          - name: Set up Node.js
            uses: actions/setup-node@v4
            with:
              node-version: 20
              cache: 'npm'

          - name: Install Dependencies
            run: npm ci

          - name: Build Static Site
            run: npm run build
    ```
  </TabItem>
</Tabs>

---

## Why Automated Guardrails Matter

Implementing these pipelines transforms documentation maintenance from a reactive chore into a proactive system:

* **Eliminating Editorial Fatigue:** Writers don't need to manually proofread for passive voice or style compliance; Vale handles it objectively.
* **Zero Dead Links:** Technical manuals lose credibility the moment a link fails. Lychee guarantees that every reference remains functional.
* **Confidence in Merges:** Because the CI build acts as a strict gatekeeper, broken MDX tags or invalid frontmatter schemas can *never* accidentally make it into production.

<Aside type="tip">
You can inspect the complete workflow files inside the `.github/workflows/` directory of the project repository to view the full pipeline configuration.
</Aside>

## Daily Authoring Lifecycle

When a subject matter expert or writer contributes to the knowledge base, they follow a streamlined four-step publishing routine:

<Steps>
  1. **Log In to the Admin Panel**
     Navigate to your deployment URL (`/admin/`) and authenticate securely using your GitHub account.
  2. **Select or Create a Document**
     Choose an existing article from the *Architecture Guides* or *Component Library* collections, or click **New Article** to start fresh.
  3. **Draft with Structure**
     Input your frontmatter metadata (`title`, `description`) and compose the core content using the rich-text editor or raw Markdown mode.
  4. **Publish & Trigger PR**
     Click **Publish**. Sveltia CMS automatically commits the changes to a new branch and opens a pull request for automated review.
</Steps>

## Authoring Dos and Don'ts

To prevent build failures and keep styling uniform across the entire documentation site, keep these core rules in mind:

<CardGrid>

  </Card>
  <Card title="DON'T: Break Frontmatter" icon="close">
    Never delete or alter required frontmatter fields like `title` or `description`. Missing fields will cause the Astro content schema validation to fail in CI.
  </Card>
  <Card title="DO: Use Markdown for Formatting" icon="seti:markdown">
    Rely on standard Markdown headers (`##`, `###`), bullet points, and blockquotes rather than hardcoding HTML elements.
  </Card>
  <Card title="DON'T: Bypass Code Blocks" icon="warning">
    When including code snippets, always specify the programming language (e.g., ```javascript) so syntax highlighting renders correctly.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

Images and diagrams are critical for effective technical documentation. Sveltia CMS handles media uploads seamlessly through its built-in asset manager:

<Tabs>

The bridge between Sveltia CMS's visual interface and our Astro codebase is the **`config.yml`** file. Located in the public directory (`public/admin/config.yml`), this file defines every collection, folder path, and form field available to authors.

## The Configuration Architecture

Explore the directory setup and the underlying YAML configuration that powers the CMS admin panel.

<Tabs>
  <TabItem label="1. Admin Directory Structure" icon="seti:folder">
    *Where the CMS entry point lives in your project.*

    ```text
    public/
      admin/
        index.html      # Loads the Sveltia CMS SPA script
        config.yml      # Defines collections, fields, and Git backend
    ```
  </TabItem>

  <TabItem label="2. config.yml Code" icon="seti:yaml">
    *Mapping Markdown collections and frontmatter fields.*

    ```yaml
    backend:
      name: github
      repo: write-tim/sveltia-docs-test
      branch: main

    media_folder: src/assets
    public_folder: /src/assets

    collections:
      - name: guides
        label: Architecture Guides
        folder: src/content/docs/guides
        create: true
        fields:
          - { name: title, label: Title, widget: string }
          - { name: description, label: Description, widget: string }
          - { name: body, label: Body, widget: markdown }

      - name: components
        label: Component Library
        folder: src/content/docs/components
        create: true
        fields:
          - { name: title, label: Title, widget: string }
          - { name: description, label: Description, widget: string }
          - { name: body, label: Body, widget: markdown }
    ```
  </TabItem>

  <TabItem label="3. Connecting to Astro Zod" icon="setting">
    *Ensuring strict type safety between the CMS and Astro.*

    When authors submit content through Sveltia CMS, Astro's content collection schema validates the incoming frontmatter. If a required field (like `description`) is missing, the build fails safely in CI rather than throwing a runtime error in production.
  </TabItem>
</Tabs>

While engineers are comfortable authoring Markdown inside IDEs and pushing changes via pull requests, subject matter experts (SMEs), product managers, and technical writers often require a clean graphical interface.

## Why Sveltia CMS?

Unlike traditional enterprise CMS platforms (such as WordPress or Contentful) that require a hosted database, server infrastructure, and complex API layers, Sveltia operates entirely inside the browser as a **static single-page application (SPA)**.

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Zero Backend Required" icon="laptop">
    There is no database to maintain or server to patch. The CMS communicates directly with the GitHub API via OAuth.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Direct-to-Git Commits" icon="git">
    Every save, edit, or image upload is committed directly back to the GitHub repository as clean Markdown or MDX files.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Lightning Fast" icon="star">
    Built with modern web standards and optimized for speed, rendering large documentation collections instantly.
  </Card>
  <Card title="WYSIWYG & Raw Editing" icon="seti:markdown">
    Contributors can toggle seamlessly between a clean rich-text preview interface and raw Markdown/MDX code.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

## How the Authoring Loop Works

When an SME logs into the CMS, the underlying workflow mirrors a professional software release cycle without exposing the user to git commands:

<Steps>
  1. **Authentication**
     The user logs in securely using their GitHub credentials via the Git Gateway / OAuth provider.
  2. **Content Modification**
     The user edits an existing guide, creates a new component specimen, or uploads an optimized image.
  3. **Automated Branching & Commit**
     When the user clicks "Publish," Sveltia CMS automatically creates a dedicated patch branch, commits the file changes, and opens a Pull Request.
  4. **CI/CD Validation**
     GitHub Actions instantly runs our quality gates (Vale, Lychee, and Astro build checks) against the proposed changes.
</Steps>

## How Search Works

Search is powered by Pagefind, a search library that runs entirely locally in the user's browser. It indexes content during the static site build step, ensuring instant results without relying on external databases.

### Search Optimization Checklist

To ensure your articles rank properly in the internal search, follow these authoring best practices:

* **Descriptive Titles:** Use action-oriented titles like *How to Configure SSO* instead of *SSO Settings*.
* **Keyword-Rich Descriptions:** Pagefind gives extra weight to the frontmatter `description` field. Always include one.
* **Semantic Headings:** Always use proper Markdown headers (`##`, `###`). Pagefind anchors search results directly to individual section headings, allowing users to jump directly to the relevant step.
* **Synonyms in Introductory Text:** Include common alternate phrasing in the opening paragraph (e.g., mentioning "API tokens" alongside "API keys").

---

Because Sveltia CMS operates entirely as a static single-page application (SPA) inside the browser, it requires a secure authentication bridge to interact with GitHub's API. This connection is established using **GitHub OAuth**, ensuring that subject matter experts can safely log in, edit content, and generate pull requests using their own credentials.

---

## Architecture of Authentication

The authentication flow relies on a secure token exchange between the browser CMS client and GitHub:

<Steps>
  1. **Login Trigger**
     The user navigates to `/admin/` and clicks **Login with GitHub**.
  2. **OAuth Handshake**
     The browser redirects to GitHub's authorization page, prompting the user to grant repository access permissions.
  3. **Token Issuance**
     Upon approval, GitHub returns an OAuth access token back to the authentication gateway.
  4. **API Communication**
     Sveltia CMS uses this token to fetch files, commit changes, and open pull requests directly on behalf of the authenticated user.
</Steps>

---

## Configuring the GitHub OAuth App

To enable authentication for your repository, you must register an OAuth application within your GitHub organization or personal account settings:

<Tabs>
  <TabItem icon="github" label="1. Register Application">
    *Navigate to GitHub Settings > Developer Settings > OAuth Apps > New OAuth App.*

    * **Application Name:** `Sveltia Docs CMS (Local/Production)`
    * **Homepage URL:** `https://docs.timothyjohnsonwrites.com` (or `http://localhost:4321` for local testing)
    * **Authorization Callback URL:** `https://api.netlify.com/auth/done` (or your chosen OAuth gateway provider URL)
  </TabItem>

  <TabItem icon="seti:config" label="2. Environment Variables">
    *Securing your Client ID and Client Secret.*

    Your deployment host (such as Netlify, Vercel, or a custom OAuth server) requires two environment variables to handle the handshake securely:

    ```ini
    OAUTH_CLIENT_ID=your_github_oauth_client_id
    OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET=your_github_oauth_client_secret
    ```
  </TabItem>
</Tabs>

---

Static images of architecture flows get outdated the moment you push a code change. To keep our documentation living and breathing, this site utilizes **Mermaid.js** integrated directly through `astro-mermaid`. 

Instead of opening a design tool like Figma or Visio, our diagrams are written as pure text, version-controlled in Git, and compiled into responsive SVGs at build time.

## How to Write a Mermaid Diagram

To render a flowchart, wrap your syntax inside a standard Markdown code block and label the language as `mermaid`. 

<Steps>
1. **Define the Direction:** 
   Start your block by declaring the layout flow (e.g., `graph TD` for Top-to-Down, or `graph LR` for Left-to-Right).
2. **Declare Your Nodes:**
   Give each node a unique letter identifier and wrap its display text in the appropriate shape brackets:
   * `A[Square Box]` for standard components.
   * `B(Rounded Pill)` for entry/exit points.
   * `C{Diamond}` for conditional decision gates.
3. **Connect the Flow:**
   Use arrows (`-->`) and optional text pipes (`-->|action|`) to map out the system logic.
</Steps>

## The Aside Component

The `<Aside>` component draws the reader's attention to critical information. **Rule of thumb: If a page has more than three asides, the core text needs to be rewritten.**

*   **Tip (Green):** Use for workflow shortcuts, best practices, or optional enhancements.
*   **Caution (Yellow):** Use when an action might disrupt a workflow, cause minor data loss, or requires specific prerequisites.
*   **Danger (Red):** Use strictly for irreversible, destructive actions (e.g., deleting a repository or dropping a database).

<Aside type="danger">
Never use a Danger aside for stylistic emphasis. It is strictly reserved for critical warnings that impact system stability.
</Aside>

## Code Formatting

Documentation often requires mixing plain English with technical syntax. Use the appropriate formatting for the context:

### Inline Code
Use single backticks (` `) for inline code when referencing file names, UI button labels, or short variables within a sentence (e.g., open the `config.yml` file).

### Fenced Code Blocks
Use triple backticks for multi-line scripts or terminal commands. Always specify the language for proper syntax highlighting.

    ```javascript
    // Always include the language tag (e.g., javascript, bash, yaml)
    const greeting = "Hello, world!";
    ```
  </TabItem>
  <TabItem label="Don't" icon="close">
    ```
    Don't leave the language tag blank. It breaks the syntax highlighting!
    ```

</Tabs>

## Image & Media Guidelines

Images should clarify complex UI interactions, not replace well-written text.

1.  **Keep it Focused:** Crop screenshots to the relevant UI element. Do not upload full-desktop screenshots unless the overall context is strictly necessary.
2.  **File Formats:** Use `.png` for crisp UI screenshots and `.webp` or `.jpg` for larger, complex images.
3.  **No Text in Images:** Never embed critical instructions directly inside an image graphic. Screen readers cannot parse it, and it cannot be easily translated.
Guidelines for writing clear, approachable, and accessible software documentation.

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Great software user documentation doesn't just explain how a system works; it guides the user with clarity and empathy. This guide outlines the core principles for maintaining a consistent voice across our content strategy.

## Active Voice and Direct Action

Always write in the active voice. It is more concise, easier to translate, and clearly identifies who is performing the action. 

*   **Do:** "Click the **Save** button to apply your changes."
*   **Don't:** "The changes can be applied by clicking the Save button."

When outlining step-by-step procedures, start each step with a strong imperative verb.

## The Author Persona

Our tone should be approachable, confident, and highly readable. We want to sound like a knowledgeable colleague helping you troubleshoot at your desk.

*   **Be concise, not robotic:** Avoid overly clinical jargon when a simple word will do.
*   **Validate the user's effort:** When documenting complex workflows, it is okay to acknowledge the complexity, but always follow up with a clear path forward.
*   **Avoid colloquialisms:** Slang and idioms do not translate well for global audiences. Keep the instructions literal.

## Accessibility (a11y) Standards

Documentation is only effective if everyone can read it. Accessibility is a strict requirement for every published article.

*   **Meaningful Link Text:** Never use "Click here." Hyperlinks must describe the destination (e.g., "Read the [API Authentication Guide](#)").
*   **Descriptive Alt Text:** Every image must include `alt` text that describes the function or data shown in the screenshot, not just its literal appearance.
*   **Semantic Structure:** Do not skip heading levels (e.g., jumping from `##` to `####`). Screen readers rely on a strict heading hierarchy to navigate the page.

<Aside type="tip">
When writing alt text for UI screenshots, focus on the action the user needs to take rather than describing every element in the window.
</Aside>
The official process for drafting, reviewing, and publishing documentation.

import { Aside, Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Our documentation operates on a strict **Docs-as-Code** philosophy. This means our written content is treated with the exact same rigor, version control, and review processes as our software codebase.

There are two supported paths for authoring content: the visual **Sveltia CMS** (recommended for standard updates) and the **Local IDE** (recommended for deep structural changes). Both paths ultimately follow the exact same Git workflow.

## The Publishing Pipeline

```mermaid
graph TD;
    A[Local VS Code] -->|git push| C(GitHub Repository);
    B[Sveltia CMS] -->|Direct Commit| C;
    C -->|Webhook Trigger| D{Render CI/CD};
    D -- Invalid Frontmatter --> E[Build Fails Safely];
    D -- Passes Zod Schema --> F[Deploy to Live Site];
```

Every new article or major update must go through the following lifecycle before reaching the live site:

<Steps>

1.  **Drafting:** 
    Authors create or edit `.mdx` files either via the Sveltia CMS dashboard or locally in their IDE (like VS Code).
    
2.  **Version Control (Branching):**
    Never commit directly to the `main` branch. All work must be done on a semantic feature branch (e.g., `docs/add-sso-guide` or `fix/typo-in-faq`). 
    *(Note: Sveltia CMS handles this automatically when you use the "Editorial Workflow" setting).*

3.  **Pull Request (PR) & Review:**
    Once the draft is complete, open a Pull Request against the `main` branch. At least one peer review is required. Reviewers will check for technical accuracy, Voice & Tone compliance, and proper component usage.

4.  **Continuous Integration (CI):**
    Our Render pipeline will automatically build a staging preview of your branch. If the build fails (e.g., due to a missing frontmatter title or broken Markdown), the PR cannot be merged until the errors are resolved.

5.  **Merge & Deploy:**
    Once approved, the PR is merged into `main`. Render automatically detects this merge and deploys the new documentation to the live site within minutes.

</Steps>

<Aside type="caution">
**Frontmatter is strictly enforced.** Our CI pipeline uses Zod schemas to validate metadata. If you attempt to publish an article without a `title`, the build will fail immediately to protect the live site.
</Aside>

## Content Audits

To ensure our Knowledge Base doesn't become a graveyard of outdated information, every article must be reviewed at least once every 6 months. If a feature is deprecated in the software, its corresponding documentation must be removed or archived in the same deployment cycle.

Documentation is code. That is the foundational premise of this architecture. When you treat documentation with the same engineering rigor as application code—housed in Git repositories, written in human-readable Markdown/MDX, and validated via automated CI/CD pipelines—you eliminate the friction that causes knowledge bases to rot.

This site operates as a live specimen of that philosophy: a high-performance static site built with **Astro** and **Starlight**, coupled with a Git-backed visual CMS (**Sveltia**) so non-technical subject matter experts (SMEs) can contribute without touching a terminal.

---

## Why Docs-as-Code?

Traditional enterprise documentation often lives in siloed, proprietary tools (like Confluence or massive monolithic CMS platforms) where styling is inconsistent, version control is an afterthought, and contributions require navigating clunky WYSIWYG interfaces. 

Docs-as-Code flips that paradigm by aligning technical writing with modern software engineering workflows:

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Single Source of Truth" icon="git">
    Content lives alongside the application source code or in dedicated repositories, tracked line-by-line using Git history, branches, and pull requests.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Decoupled Authoring" icon="seti:html">
    Writers author in lightweight Markdown or via a clean Git-backed UI, while static site generators handle enterprise-grade styling and performance.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Automated Quality Gates" icon="approve-check">
    Prose linting, broken link checking, and schema validations happen automatically in the background before a single word goes live.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Zero Vendor Lock-In" icon="laptop">
    Your content is stored as open-standard plain-text files (`.md` / `.mdx`). You own your data entirely and can migrate hosting platforms at will.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

---

## The Workflow Lifecycle

Moving from an idea to published documentation follows a predictable, transparent engineering lifecycle:

<Steps>
  1. **Authoring & Editing**
     Writers draft content either locally in an IDE using Markdown or via the web-based Sveltia CMS interface.
  2. **Branching & Pull Requests**
     Changes are committed to feature branches. Opening a pull request automatically triggers a preview deployment for review.
  3. **Automated Quality Checks**
     GitHub Actions run prose linters (Vale) and link integrity checkers (Lychee) against the proposed changes.
  4. **Merge & Deploy**
     Once approved and checks pass, merging into the `main` branch triggers an automated build that publishes globally via CDN.
</Steps>

---

## Bridging the Gap: Engineers + SMEs

One of the historic challenges of Docs-as-Code has been accessibility. While engineers love Git and Markdown, subject matter experts—such as product managers, customer success leads, and executives—often struggle with terminal commands and pull requests.

This project solves that divide through **Sveltia CMS**:

* **For Engineers:** Complete control over components, styling, routing, and automated pipelines using Astro and GitHub.
* **For SMEs:** A clean, zero-config web interface that commits changes directly back to the Git repository as clean Markdown files behind the scenes.

<Aside type="tip">
You can explore the live CMS configuration and authoring guide in the **Sveltia CMS Manual** section of the sidebar to see how this dual-audience workflow is configured.
</Aside>

## The End-to-End Lifecycle

The diagram below outlines the five major milestones a documentation update traverses before reaching readers:

<Steps>
  1. **Authoring & Commit**
     The author writes content in Markdown/MDX, either locally in an IDE or through the browser-based Sveltia CMS interface, and commits to a feature branch.
  2. **Version Control & PR Creation**
     The branch is pushed to GitHub, automatically triggering a Pull Request against the `main` production branch.
  3. **Automated Quality Gates**
     GitHub Actions spins up a clean runner environment to execute prose linting (Vale), link integrity checks (Lychee), and a static site build validation.
  4. **Human Review & Merge**
     Once automated checks pass and reviewers approve the changes, the PR is merged into `main`.
  5. **Global Edge Deployment**
     The merge triggers a production build that publishes the compiled static assets globally via a high-performance content delivery network (CDN).
</Steps>

## Architectural Touchpoints

Every stage of this journey is guarded by automated tools designed to eliminate human error and manual overhead:

<CardGrid>

  <Card title="CI/CD Runners (GitHub Actions)" icon="approve-check">

    Pre-renders high-performance HTML/CSS and optimizes images at build time, eliminating runtime server latency.

    Serves static assets from servers physically closest to the reader for instantaneous load times worldwide.

Building a modern Docs-as-Code ecosystem requires balancing two opposing forces: **developer velocity** (speed, flexibility, automation) and **author accessibility** (simplicity, clean interfaces, low friction). 

This project achieves that balance by pairing a bleeding-edge static site engine with a Git-backed visual content management system.

---

## The Technology Stack

Every tool in the pipeline was selected for performance, standards compliance, and zero proprietary lock-in.

| Layer | Technology | Purpose |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Framework** | Astro & Starlight | High-performance static site generation with a built-in, accessible documentation layout. |
| **Content Engine** | MDX | Markdown extended with native support for interactive UI components and widgets. |
| **Visual CMS** | Sveltia CMS | A lightweight, Git-gateway CMS that lets non-technical contributors edit content via a GUI. |
| **Version Control** | GitHub | Hosting repository, pull request reviews, and issue tracking. |
| **CI/CD Automation** | GitHub Actions | Automated build previews, link validation, and prose linting on every commit. |

## Repository Structure

The project follows a standard Astro project layout, separating reusable components, design tokens, and documentation content into dedicated directories:

<FileTree>
- .github/workflows/       # CI/CD pipelines (Lint, Link Check, Build)
- public/                  # Static assets, logos, and favicons
- src/
  - assets/                # Images and graphics optimized by Astro
  - components/            # Custom interactive widgets and specimens
  - content/
    - docs/                # All Markdown/MDX documentation pages
      - components/        # Component library specimen articles
      - guides/            # Architecture and workflow documentation
      - cms/               # Sveltia CMS configuration manual
    - config.ts            # Content collections schema definition
  - styles/                # Custom CSS styling and design tokens
- astro.config.mjs         # Starlight and integration configuration
- package.json             # Project dependencies and npm scripts
</FileTree>

## Git Branching Strategy

To maintain stability while allowing rapid iterations, the repository utilizes a streamlined branching model inspired by GitHub Flow:

<Tabs>
  <TabItem label="main" icon="seti:git">
    **The Production Branch**
    * Always reflects what is currently deployed live to production.
    * Direct commits are locked; code and content enter via reviewed Pull Requests.
    * Every successful merge automatically triggers a production build.
  </TabItem>
  <TabItem label="feature / patch" icon="seti:branch">
    **Working Branches**
    * Branch naming convention: `feature/short-description` or `fix/issue-name`.
    * Used for drafting new guides, updating components, or adjusting CSS tokens.
    * Opening a pull request against `main` immediately fires automated CI preview builds.
  </TabItem>
</Tabs>

<Aside type="tip">
When contributors write via Sveltia CMS, the application automatically handles the underlying Git mechanics—committing changes to a dedicated patch branch and opening a pull request behind the scenes.
</Aside>

## The "Specimen & Source" Pattern

As seen throughout the Component Library section of this site, architectural documentation often suffers from a disconnect between theory and implementation. 

This project solves that via the **Specimen & Source** pattern:
1. **The Live Specimen:** Renders the actual, interactive UI component using Starlight's built-in design system.
2. **The Source Code:** Displays the exact raw MDX markup required to generate it inside collapsible tabs.
3. **The Authoring Guide:** Explains how subject matter experts interact with the component inside Sveltia CMS.

By keeping the documentation *about* the components inside the same codebase as the components themselves, code drift is entirely eliminated.
